claims.claim: Cadden says 'A Description of Earthsea' is told from outside the world of Earthsea.
claims.source: Mike Cadden, Ursula K. Le Guin Beyond Genre (Routledge, 2005)
claims.quote: is told from outside the world of Earthsea

claims.claim: Cadden says the book is true to the voice of the anthropologist examining the ways of the Kesh.
claims.source: Mike Cadden, Ursula K. Le Guin Beyond Genre (Routledge, 2005)
claims.quote: the voice of the anthropologist examining the ways

claims.claim: Cadden says the book does not rely on any one narrating voice in the presentation of this anthropological text.
claims.source: Mike Cadden, Ursula K. Le Guin Beyond Genre (Routledge, 2005)
claims.quote: in the presentation of this anthropological text

claims.claim: An essay in that volume notes that Ai sees each keystone in the city of Erhenrang joined by red cement.
claims.source: An essay in Olander and Greenberg, eds., Ursula K. Le Guin (Taplinger, 1979)
claims.quote: each keystone he sees in the city of Erhenrang

claims.claim: Spivack says the language of A Wizard of Earthsea is largely Anglo-Saxon in diction.
claims.source: Charlotte Spivack, Ursula K. Le Guin (Twayne, 1984)

claims.claim: Spivack says the alliteration in A Wizard of Earthsea is pervasive, recalling the oral tradition.
claims.source: Charlotte Spivack, Ursula K. Le Guin (Twayne, 1984)
claims.quote: The alliteration is pervasive, recalling the oral tradition

claims.claim: Spivack says Le Guin draws on her anthropological background to create cultural concepts for her imaginary worlds.
claims.source: Charlotte Spivack, Ursula K. Le Guin (Twayne, 1984)
claims.quote: Drawing on her anthropological background, Le Guin is able

claims.claim: Spivack says the vocabulary of Le Guin's poems is straightforward, with a diction austerely avoiding the Latinate or the ornate.
claims.source: Charlotte Spivack, Ursula K. Le Guin (Twayne, 1984)
claims.quote: a diction austerely avoiding the Latinate or the ornate

claims.claim: Spivack calls the diction of those poems homely and reminiscent of Robert Frost.
claims.source: Charlotte Spivack, Ursula K. Le Guin (Twayne, 1984)
claims.quote: The homely diction is reminiscent of Robert Frost

claims.claim: Bucknall says what Le Guin says of Tolkien's style is to a certain extent true of the way she writes herself.
claims.source: Barbara J. Bucknall, Ursula K. Le Guin (Frederick Ungar, 1981)
claims.quote: is to a certain extent true of the way she

claims.claim: Bucknall says Le Guin's style varies from book to book and from character to character.
claims.source: Barbara J. Bucknall, Ursula K. Le Guin (1981)
claims.quote: which varies from book to book and from character

claims.claim: Bucknall praises Le Guin for writing poetically while resisting the temptation to overwrite.
claims.source: Barbara J. Bucknall, Ursula K. Le Guin (1981)
claims.quote: while resisting the temptation to overwrite

claims.claim: Bucknall says Le Guin's style does not have the stately and heroic tone of The Lord of the Rings.
claims.source: Barbara J. Bucknall, Ursula K. Le Guin (1981)
claims.quote: does not have the stately and heroic tone

claims.claim: Le Guin writes that Tolkien writes a plain, clear English.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973), quoted in Bucknall (1981)
claims.quote: Tolkien writes a plain, clear English

claims.claim: Le Guin writes that Tolkien's vocabulary is not striking.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973), quoted in Bucknall (1981)
